title: We Need to Stop Cold Calling
author: Claudia Lewis
summary: Claudia Lewis argues that the widely-used technique of Cold Calling has a real flaw, but it isn't the technique itself -- it's that teachers routinely misapply it by picking students at random. Drawing on classroom observations of lollysticks, name-picking widgets, laminated seating plans, and even balls thrown to students, she shows how a textbook-perfect 'question, pause, name' structure still leaves at least one anxious student thinking 'what if it's me?' instead of thinking about the answer. Lewis reframes Cold Calling as fundamentally a ratio technique -- its value lies in the pause before a name is given, which forces the whole class to think, not in the randomness of who gets picked. Her proposed fix is to rename and reframe the practice as 'targeted questioning': teachers should already know who they're going to ask before the question is even finished, while pretending otherwise, and should only pick students they're confident can answer or who are in a strong enough culture of error to handle a mistake safely.
points: Lewis's key distinction -- cold calling itself isn't the problem, random selection is -- reframes a heated debate about a specific technique into a more precise critique of how it's implemented.

She catalogues five different randomising mechanisms she's observed in real lessons (lollysticks, a hat, a PowerPoint widget, a seating-plan cross-off system, and a thrown ball), grounding the critique in direct classroom observation rather than theory.

Her core mechanism claim -- that cold calling is fundamentally a 'ratio technique' whose value comes from the pause before the name, not the randomness of the name itself -- gives teachers a concrete design principle to apply.

The proposed rename to 'targeted questioning' comes with an explicit behavioural rule: a teacher should already know who they're asking before finishing the question, and should only put a student on the spot if reasonably confident they can answer.
quotes: As a profession - perhaps driven by parents - we are increasingly concerned with the anxiety levels of our students.
But the problem is not cold calling, per se. The problem is picking students randomly.
In every case, the questioning structure was near-flawless. Textbook "question, pause, name". 10 out of 10.

Cold call, fundamentally is a ratio technique. By phrasing the question in the manner question, pause, name, you are ensuring that during that pause, every student has the opportunity to think about the answer.
If you want to know if a student or students know something, use mini whiteboard - you get a lot more data in a much shorter time.
Instead of cold call, we should return to calling it targeted questioning.
When I ask a question in class, I know, before the question is even out of my mouth, which student is getting called on, I just pretend that I don't.
Stop picking students randomly to answer questions to the whole class, instead know in advance which student you're targeting and fake it.
